newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Sept 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Sept 29.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- BRITISH GAS TO QUIT SCOTLAND

British Gas is in talks with the electricity company Scottish Hydro about selling its gas supply business in Scotland and the north of England for 250 million stg. The two sides have asked the Office of Fair Trading for guidance. The deal is seen as a move by British Gas to escape the financial and regulatory pressures which beset it.
-- TRANSCO DISPUTE HEADS TO MMC

The rejection by British Gas of price cuts imposed on TransCo, its pipeline business, by industry regulator Ofgas, will trigger an inquiry by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. The price cap would have taken 650 million stg off annual turnover and cut customer bills by 28 stg. It decided that Ofgas's terms are still too stringent.
-- SFO TWILIGHT RAID ON YOUNG'S HOME
The Serious Fraud Office has raided the home of former Morgan Grenfell unit trust manager Peter Young on Friday evening.

Young was not charged but a number of documents were taken away. The raid came the day after director of the SFO George Staple decided to launch a criminal investigation into Young's activities as manager of Morgan's European Growth Fund.
-- HATCHET MEN SEEK NEW KENWOOD BLEND

The maker of food mixers Kenwood Appliances has been boarded by two dissident shareholders, Julian Treger and Brian Myerson, who plan to shake up the group and unlock its value. The two men have built up a 7.74 per cent stake in Kenwood in the past six weeks. Chief executive Tim Beech is now under increasing City pressure after the group issued a profits warning at it annual meeting.
-- STORES CHECK OUT CHILD LABOUR

J Sainsbury and the Co-op are to launch a campaign to uncover child labour exploitation among Third World suppliers. The supermarket chains have signed a pact with the Fairtrade Foundation, a charity controlled by bodies such as Christian Aid and Oxfam.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- HOUSE OF FRASER TO AXE 1,000 AS STORES CLOSE

1,000 jobs are to be axed at the department-store chain House of Fraser after it closes 10 stores as a result of a review of business by new chief executive John Coleman. A restructuring charge of 30 million stg will be made within the next year. Interim results, due this week, will justify Coleman's measures.
-- OFT TO APPROVE BA -US ALLIANCE

It is believed that the Office of Fair Trading is to recommend that the government clears the planned merger between British Airways and American Airlines on conditions that will be accepted by both carriers. The DTI will require that BA and American transfer some take-off and landing slots at Heathrow to new entrants. Both government and industry executives believe the conditions will be accepted by both parties.
-- CONSUMER BOOM BRINGS SURGE IN RETAILING JOBS

According to the latest Sunday Times/Manpower quarterly Jobwatch, jobs in retailing are increasing at their fastest rate for six years, thus confirming the strength of the consumer upturn. A fourth-quarter upturn in retailing jobs is normal because of Christmas shopping but the latest figure is much stronger than a year ago.
-- NEW SE TRADING SYSTEM DELAYED

The Stock Exchange is to publish detailed plans for its electronic trading and order-matching system. It is expected to say the switch to order-driven trading for FT-SE 100 index shares will be delayed from next summer to the last quarter of 1997. The delay is caused by Treasury amendments to stamp-duty relief, after consultations with the Securities and Investments Board.
-- ROVER PURSUES ENGINE PLANT AID

BMW and its Rover subsidiary are asking the government for 70 million stg in aid to help fund a 450 million stg British engine factory that would secure thousands of jobs in the Midlands and boost the motor industry's export performance. According to Whitehall insiders, Ian Lang, board of trade president and DTI officials will respond to the request soon.
THE OBSERVER
-- INDUSTRY LINKS TAINT GREEN TAX

Environmental groups have attacked the first ever green tax, due to be introduced on Tuesday, over links between the body set up to monitor funds given to green projects and waste disposal companies. The watchdog is headed by the Earl of Cranbrook, a Tory peer, who receives 7,000 stg a year from Shanks and McEwan, one of Britain's largest wasted disposal firms, for chairing their environmental advisory board.
-- TREASURY MOVES IN WITH DEVELOPER

The Treasury is set to temporarily move into central London offices owned by Chelsfield, the property company, despite over 11 million available square foot of empty government property. Chelsfield is one of the companies in the consortium redeveloping the Treasury building. The vacant buildings cost taxpayers 130 million stg a year in rent and rates.
-- INTEREST IN THISTLE FLOAT MOUNTS AFTER THORNY START

Hotel group Thistle is expected to be priced at the lower end of the 170 to 210 pence stg price range when it comes to the market this week. This is seen as a relief to sponsors after predictions that the group would flop. Shares have attracted interest from private investors. However, not all UK institutions have registered an interest.
-- GOVERNMENT TO FACE DEMANDS FOR RETURN OF NATIONAL BUS PENSION SURPLUS

The government will face demands in Parliament to return the 200 million stg surplus taken from the National Bus Company pension scheme during privatisation. Dr Julian Farrand, the pensions Ombudsman, ruled that trustees to the scheme should take steps to recover the surplus. The Department of Transport says it is still studying the ombudsman's decision.
-- MORE TO BE NAMED IN WICKES SCANDAL

The investigation into accounting irregularities at Wickes, the DIY retailer, is to implicate a further four current or former senior executives. Shareholders will have to wait another week before names are revealed. A letter detailing the findings of accountant Price Waterhouse and solicitor Linklaters and Paine is not expected until next week after the investigation took longer than expected.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- NORWICH UNION FLOAT TO GO AHEAD

The country's second largest mutual insurance company, Norwich Union, is to confirm it intends to go ahead with a stock market flotation, which will capitalise the company at four billion stg and bring an average windfall of 500 stg for its three million life policyholders.
-- FIRE TRUCK FIRM ON THE BRINK

Simon Engineering, Britain's last manufacturer of aerial ladder trucks for fire brigades is refusing to take new orders in a move which is seen as marking the end of the domestic business. Industry sources say the company is winding down its loss-making Access UK operation so it can get a better price for the larger and healthier US division.
-- PEPSI RELAUNCH FAILS TO LIFT OFF

Pepsico has admitted that its 500 million dollar "Blue" relaunch has been a disappointment. The company announced it would take a restructuring charge of 525 million stg to pay for losses in its Latin American bottling subsidiary and fund a company-wide strategic reorganisation. It warned that reconstructuring could lead to job losses for employees in Europe and change its relationship with bottlers and customers.
-- PRESSURE MOUNTS ON EUROTUNNEL BANKS

Eurotunnel, the Channel Tunnel operator, is set to miss the deadline for restructuring of its 8.5 billion stg debt on Monday. This increases the pressure on its 225 banks from the French courts to reach an agreement with the operator. The mandate of court appointed mediators will expire tomorrow as banks continue to argue over rescue terms.
-- SFO LAUNCHES THIRD BRENT WALKER FRAUD TRIAL

The SFO returns to the courts on Monday when Donald Anderson, former finance director of Goldcrest films, appears in court as part of the second trial of former executives of Brent Walker, the debt-laden pubs to betting group. Mr Anderson will face the charge of attempting to prevent the course of justice in film and other dealings at the Brent Walker subsidiary between August 1988 and October 1990.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- UNITED TO BEAT CARLTON FOR HTV

United News and Media, the Express Newspapers and Anglia TV group, is set to beat Carlton Communications in a 300 million stg takeover bid for HTV. This could trigger a chain of multi- million pound stg deals and counter deals when the law changes in November to allow TV and newspaper companies to merge. A United takeover of HTV would increase it share of ITV advertising revenues to 25 per cent and boost its power throughout the network.
-- FACIA BOSS IS SUED FOR 34 MILLION STG

Founder of the collapsed Facia group Stephen Hinchliffe is being sued for 34 million stg by administrators of part of his former empire. The claim is for money alleged to have been moved from Facia Footwear, Wisebird and Cityscan into other retail operations. Administrators also want to recover money allegedly paid into Matchmaker Holdings, one of Hinchliffe's private companies, and Sheffield United Football Club, where he was vice chairman.
-- NEW LOANS TO BOOST CASH-STARVED CHARITIES

The Charities Aid Foundation is set to launch a loan scheme designed to boost British charities. The initiative is to be called Investors in Society and will allow businesses and individuals to lend, rather than give, money to charities on an interest-free basis. Some of the country's big companies have welcomed the idea and pledged support.
-- EURO MONEY TO HELP UK FIRMS

A top Brussels official has said that the European Loan Scheme for Employment, a one billion stg EU scheme that is opposed in the UK, will be approved in weeks. It will pave the way for a second scheme in November to encourage employment, growth and competitiveness. The proposal will use 21 million stg of the EC's 1996 budget to guarantee 800 million stg loans from the European Investment Fund.
-- RNLI MAY CAST AILING FUND MANAGER ADRIFT

Leading charities are considering sacking PDFM, the City fund manager. The Royal National Lifeboat Institution is reviewing its relationship with the PDFM after the company's poor investment performance over the past 18 months. Others, including the Rank Foundation, are reviewing PDFM's seven billion stg bet that world stock markets would crash soon. The fund manager has converted 15 per cent of its funds under management into cash ahead of the anticipated crash, more than its rivals.
